analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes outright.
analysis.headline: A bill to eliminate the federal estate tax, backed by 31 Republican senators, died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently eliminated the federal taxes on wealth passed at death and on large gifts, which in 1996 raised just under 1% of all federal revenue. Only estates larger than the exemption — several hundred thousand dollars at the time — pay these taxes at all, so the direct benefit would have gone to heirs of the largest estates. Supporters argued repeal would spare family businesses and farms from forced sales and spur growth; the bill never advanced beyond one Senate Finance Committee hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs and families holding estates large enough to owe estate tax — those exceeding the exemption, which was several hundred thousand dollars per person at the time — would pay nothing on inheritances. Owners of family businesses and farms who might otherwise sell assets to pay the tax would also benefit. Wealthy taxpayers making large lifetime gifts would no longer owe gift tax, and estates could skip generations without the generation-skipping tax.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax for deaths and transfers after enactment.

Supporters argued the taxes force small businesses and farms to liquidate assets to pay the bill, and cited an analysis claiming repeal would add $77 billion to economic output and create more than 1 million jobs over seven years.

The bill's findings noted these taxes produced less than 1% of total federal revenue in fiscal 1996, arguing they raised little money while costing families billions in estate-planning and legal fees.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would lose the roughly 1% of revenue these taxes raise — a cost eventually shared by all taxpayers through other taxes, borrowing, or reduced services. The benefit would be concentrated on the wealthiest families, since estates below the exemption threshold already paid nothing. Estate lawyers, accountants, and trust businesses would lose the market the tax supports.

drawbacks.text: The tax cut would flow almost entirely to the largest estates: families with estates below the exemption level paid no estate tax already, so repeal transfers revenue away from the Treasury to the heirs of the wealthiest households.
The bill's own findings concede these taxes raised revenue — under 1% of the federal total — which would have to be replaced through other taxes, more borrowing, or smaller government spending.
Repeal would take effect immediately on enactment, applying to all deaths and gifts after the signing date, with no transition or phase-in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real benefit to a small group — families facing estate-tax bills on large businesses, farms, and estates — and eliminated genuine planning burdens that the bill text itself describes as costing billions. But because estates under the exemption paid nothing, nearly all of the forgone revenue would have gone to heirs of the largest estates, with the cost spread across every taxpayer. Weighing a broad, diffuse cost against a concentrated benefit, the design favored wealth at the top far more than it helped ordinary families.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, which held one hearing in April 1997, and it never got a markup, a floor vote, or companion action before Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl introduced the Family Heritage Preservation Act on January 21, 1997, with 14 original Republican cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
Thirty Republican senators ultimately cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor listed was a Republican.
The Finance Committee held hearings on April 10, 1997, but the bill was never reported out of committee and never received a vote in the Senate or House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal Treasury kept the revenue from estate and gift taxes, and the largest estates continued to pay them. Estate-planning lawyers and trust businesses also kept the market the tax supports.

for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes and recruited 14 original cosponsors.

for.name: 30 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the estate tax repeal bill.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Sen. William Roth, R-DE)
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing in April 1997 but never voted the bill out of committee, leaving it to die without a floor vote.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor in the two years after it was referred to committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the bill stalled in committee under a Republican-led Senate and never reached a floor vote.

industries.note: Only estates above the exemption threshold owe the tax, so repeal's direct benefit is a concentrated transfer to heirs of the largest estates, funded by revenue the Treasury would have to replace from other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning, trust, and accounting services
industries.note: The bill's own findings describe families hiring 'legions of tax accountants and lawyers' to avoid these taxes; full repeal would eliminate much of that business. Its loss would be a saving to families, not a cost.

The bill was pitched as relief for small businesses and farms that must sell assets to pay estate taxes, a benefit that would have reached the minority of family enterprises large enough to owe the tax.
